# HyperFund/HyperVerse: Investigation of the Alleged Crypto Fraud Network

## Executive assessment

The evidence supports the assessment that HyperFund and its later identities—HyperVerse and HyperNation—operated as an alleged crypto-enabled pyramid and Ponzi structure rather than as a legitimate cryptocurrency-mining or metaverse enterprise. The alleged model combined four mutually reinforcing components:

1. **Investment packages promising unusually high, largely passive returns**;
2. **Multi-level recruitment incentives that rewarded promoters for bringing in investors**;
3. **Repeated rebranding when the project encountered withdrawal and credibility problems**; and
4. **Public-facing credibility tactics, including celebrity endorsements, founder narratives, and a purported CEO whose identity and qualifications could not be substantiated.**

The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) alleged that the network raised more than **$1.7 billion**, while the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) and CNBC described the alleged criminal scheme as approximately **$1.89 billion to $1.9 billion**. These differences likely reflect different calculation methods, periods, or evidentiary bases rather than a fundamentally different case. The figures should therefore be reported as competing official or contemporaneous estimates, not reconciled as a single confirmed amount.

The strongest evidence comes from the SEC’s filed complaint and the DOJ’s case page. Those sources are government records, although the SEC complaint contains allegations and the DOJ emphasizes that criminal defendants are presumed innocent. The Guardian provides important investigative reporting concerning the purported HyperVerse CEO, Steven Reece Lewis, but its findings should be distinguished from judicially established facts.

## Sources and evidentiary status

For clarity, the supplied materials are identified as follows:

- **S1 — CNBC**, January 29, 2024: reporting on DOJ criminal charges and related SEC action.  
- **S2 — DOJ**, HyperFund and Associated Cases: official case page, including charges, case status, victim information, and later docket updates.  
- **S3 — The Guardian**, January 4, 2024: investigative reporting on the identity and credentials of “Steven Reece Lewis.”  
- **S4 — SEC**, January 29, 2024: filed civil complaint against Xue Samuel Lee and Brenda Indah Chunga.

The SEC complaint is not a final judgment. It states the SEC’s allegations and requested remedies. Similarly, an indictment or criminal complaint is not proof of guilt. The DOJ page expressly reiterates the presumption of innocence ([DOJ, 2026](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases)).

## Network identity and chronology

### HyperFund and the HyperTech Group

According to the SEC complaint, the HyperTech Group launched HyperFund in approximately June 2020. The group was presented as a blockchain conglomerate associated with Blockchain Global, HyperCash, CollinStar Capital, and DigitalX. The alleged purpose was to create a decentralized-finance ecosystem and generate returns for participants through cryptocurrency-related activity ([SEC, 2024, pp. 2, 5–7](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The SEC alleged that HyperFund was not an isolated product but part of a broader promotional network. HyperFund was subsequently rebranded as **HyperVerse** in or around December 2021 and then as **HyperNation** in or around May 2022 ([SEC, 2024, pp. 5–6](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)). The branding changed from decentralized finance, to a metaverse, and finally to a masked, quasi-political “decentralized government” concept. The underlying investment and recruitment logic, however, allegedly remained substantially similar.

### Chronology of major developments

| Period | Development | Evidentiary significance |
|---|---|---|
| June 2020 | HyperFund launched by the HyperTech Group | Establishes the alleged starting point of the network ([SEC, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)) |
| 2020–2021 | Memberships marketed with daily rewards and referral incentives | Indicates alleged Ponzi and pyramid mechanics ([SEC, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)) |
| July 2021 or late 2021/early 2022 | Withdrawal problems began, depending on the source and definition of “blocking” | Shows an important timeline discrepancy ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)) |
| December 5, 2021 | HyperVerse launch introduced “Steven Reece Lewis” as CEO | Key credibility and identity issue ([SEC, 2024, pp. 13–14](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)) |
| May 2022 | HyperVerse rebranded as HyperNation | Indicates continuation through a new narrative ([SEC, 2024, pp. 15–16](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)) |
| November 2022 | HOO Exchange reportedly stopped functioning and investors could no longer redeem investments | Marks the alleged effective collapse ([SEC, 2024, p. 16](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)) |
| January 29, 2024 | DOJ criminal charges, Chunga guilty plea, and SEC civil action announced | Marks formal U.S. enforcement activity ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases)) |

## Alleged Ponzi mechanics

### Promised returns

The central product was a “membership” purchased with cryptocurrency, especially Tether, or in some cases with fiat currency. The SEC alleged that membership levels included amounts such as **$300, $500, $1,000, and $10,000**, represented internally as HyperUnits ([SEC, 2024, pp. 8–9](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

Investors were allegedly promised passive returns of approximately **0.5% to 1% per day**, with the possibility of tripling the original investment over 600 days. HyperFund claimed that these payments were supported by large-scale cryptocurrency mining. The SEC alleged that no such mining activity existed at the scale represented and that the returns lacked a legitimate revenue basis ([SEC, 2024, pp. 2–3, 19–21](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The mathematical structure itself was a major warning sign. A daily return of 0.5% compounded over time is extraordinarily high, while a promise of a 300% return over 600 days implies a substantial and continuous funding requirement. The SEC alleged that investor withdrawals were paid with deposits from later investors rather than with revenue from mining or another productive enterprise ([SEC, 2024, pp. 3, 24–26](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

### Internal accounting and withdrawal barriers

The scheme allegedly used internal accounting units called **HyperUnits**. Although the units were shown as having a nominal value linked to the amount deposited, withdrawals required conversion through another crypto asset, Molecular Future or **MOF**, and then through the HOO Exchange. The SEC alleged that MOF’s market value was not pegged to the nominal HyperUnit value and had fallen to approximately **$0.00001949** by September 4, 2023, based on the last available price data cited in the complaint ([SEC, 2024, pp. 11–12](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

This architecture allegedly allowed the platform to display account balances that appeared valuable while making actual redemption difficult or economically destructive. The SEC further alleged that, by February or March 2022, investors were generally unable to withdraw rewards, and that the HOO Exchange ceased functioning by November 2022 ([SEC, 2024, pp. 14–16](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

### Pyramid and recruitment mechanics

The alleged Ponzi element concerned the source of funds for promised returns; the alleged pyramid element concerned the recruitment structure. HyperFund reportedly offered “Community Rewards,” “VIP Rewards,” and “Global Rewards.” Community rewards allegedly extended through as many as **20 levels** of a recruiter’s downline. The system also promised additional rewards based on team investment volumes and promoter rank ([SEC, 2024, pp. 9–11](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

Promoters were encouraged to reinvest rewards rather than withdraw them. This would have had two effects: it created the appearance of continuing account growth and reduced immediate demands on the system’s available liquidity. The SEC alleged that Chunga encouraged “rebuys,” while the Guardian described similar incentives to keep funds inside the platform ([SEC, 2024, pp. 10–11](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [Martin, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

## Public promoters and recruitment

### Brenda Chunga

Brenda Chunga, also known as **“Bitcoin Beautee,”** was described by the SEC as one of HyperFund’s leading promoters and an important figure in its U.S. operations. The SEC alleged that she reached the highest promoter rank, “VIP 5 STAR,” after generating at least **$5 million in new investment volume** in approximately six months ([SEC, 2024, pp. 3, 11–13](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The SEC alleged that Chunga received approximately **$3.7 million**, consisting of roughly **$2.5 million** withdrawn through the platform and approximately **$1.1 million** obtained directly from investors. The complaint alleges that she used proceeds for luxury goods, property, vehicles, and recruitment-oriented displays of wealth ([SEC, 2024, pp. 12–13](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

Chunga pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud, according to CNBC and the DOJ case page. She also agreed to settle related SEC charges, including disgorgement and civil penalties to be determined or imposed through the civil process ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases)).

### Sam Lee

Sam Lee, also known as **Xue Samuel Lee**, was identified by the DOJ and SEC as an Australian national residing in Dubai and an alleged co-founder of HyperFund. The SEC alleged that he remained centrally involved throughout HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation, including appearing at the HyperVerse launch and later communicating with investors about possible recovery plans ([SEC, 2024, pp. 2, 6–8, 16](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

The SEC complaint also alleges that Lee knew, or was reckless in not knowing, that promoters were falsely describing large-scale mining operations. In an audio call cited by the SEC, Lee allegedly said the group had stopped owning mining machines after 2019 because mining was not profitable. This allegation is significant because it directly conflicts with promotional claims that warehouses were continuously mining cryptocurrencies and generating millions in revenue ([SEC, 2024, pp. 20–21](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

Lee was charged criminally with conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud, but the supplied sources do not establish a final criminal conviction. He was also named in the SEC’s civil complaint ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

## Rebranding as a continuity strategy

The rebrandings appear, based on the evidence, to have served more than a marketing function. HyperFund became HyperVerse during a period when investors were reportedly experiencing withdrawal difficulties. HyperVerse then became HyperNation after withdrawal problems persisted. The new narratives changed—from decentralized finance to a virtual metaverse and then to a masked alternative society—but continued to involve memberships, rewards, and recruitment.

This pattern is consistent with an assessment that the brands were used to preserve investor engagement and provide explanations for operational failures. However, the sources do not conclusively establish the subjective intent behind each rebranding. The SEC alleges continuity across the brands, while the Guardian reports that a promoter described HyperNation as “one big entity” with HyperVerse and the earlier projects ([SEC, 2024, pp. 13–16](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [Martin, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

## The questionable CEO persona

### “Steven Reece Lewis”

HyperVerse introduced a person named **Steven Reece Lewis** as its CEO during a December 5, 2021 online launch. Promotional materials attributed to him included degrees from the University of Leeds and the University of Cambridge, employment at Goldman Sachs, the sale of a web-development company to Adobe, and the creation of an information-technology startup ([Martin, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

The Guardian reported that neither university could locate a record of a person by that name, that no relevant Companies House or SEC records were found, and that Adobe had no public filing showing the alleged acquisition. The Guardian also reported that Goldman Sachs could not locate a record of his employment. These findings do not independently prove that the person in the video had no identity, but they strongly undermine the credentials presented to investors ([Martin, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

The SEC went further in its complaint, alleging that “Steven Reece Lewis” was a fabricated character and that the person shown was a paid actor residing in Bangkok. The SEC alleged that Lee knew or was reckless in not knowing that the purported CEO was not a genuine CEO ([SEC, 2024, pp. 14, 21–22](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)). Because this assertion appears in a complaint, it remains an allegation unless established through adjudication.

### Celebrity endorsements

HyperVerse also used short endorsement videos from figures including Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass. The Guardian reported that the videos promoted HyperVerse and its leadership but did not refer directly to investments or money. The Guardian further noted that the celebrities were available through Cameo and that there was no suggestion they understood the alleged business model when recording the messages ([Martin, 2024](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)).

These endorsements therefore appear to have functioned primarily as **borrowed credibility**. They could make the project appear socially validated without necessarily providing evidence of its finances, technology, or regulatory status.

## Contradictions and unresolved issues

### Amount allegedly raised

The SEC complaint states that HyperFund raised more than **$1.7 billion**. The DOJ and CNBC describe approximately **$1.89 billion or $1.9 billion**. The difference should not be treated as an error without additional records. It may reflect different periods, transaction datasets, or rounding conventions ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

### Timing of withdrawal restrictions

CNBC reports the DOJ allegation that withdrawals began to be blocked in July 2021. The SEC complaint says investors experienced difficulty during November or December 2021, could not generally withdraw by February or March 2022, and were unable to redeem investments by November 2022. These accounts may refer to different stages—partial restrictions, technical problems, or complete suspension—but the supplied evidence does not resolve the discrepancy ([S1](https://www.cnbc.com/2024/01/29/doj-and-sec-unveil-charges-in-1point9-billion-cryptocurrency-fraud-scheme.html); [S4](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)).

### Legal status

Chunga’s guilty plea is reported by the DOJ and CNBC. The supplied DOJ page also states that Rodney Burton was sentenced on July 23, 2026, to 32 months’ imprisonment and three years of supervised release. By contrast, the supplied materials do not establish a final conviction for Lee. Criminal charges against Lee and Burton, and civil allegations against Lee, must therefore be treated according to their different procedural statuses ([S2](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases)).

## Conclusion

The most credible synthesis of the evidence is that HyperFund/HyperVerse allegedly used a classic recruitment-dependent financial structure wrapped in changing cryptocurrency and metaverse narratives. The promised daily returns created the economic attraction; the multi-level rewards system generated recruitment; public promoters converted the model into social proof; rebranding helped maintain continuity during operational distress; and the purported CEO, celebrity videos, founder biographies, and corporate affiliations supplied an appearance of legitimacy.

The evidence is particularly persuasive where independent promotional claims are contrasted with the SEC’s detailed allegations: alleged mining revenues versus Lee’s alleged acknowledgment that the group had exited mining; claimed corporate credentials versus DigitalX’s reported disavowal; and a celebrated CEO persona versus investigative findings that the identity and qualifications could not be verified. In my assessment, the sources collectively support describing the network as an alleged crypto Ponzi/pyramid operation that used branding and credibility theater to delay investor skepticism and sustain recruitment. They do not, however, justify presenting every allegation as a final judicial finding.
